opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it came out of a frustration we kept running into in the lab. If you look at how robot learning has progressed, the bottleneck has always been data. Teleoperation gives you really high-quality, embodiment-matched demonstrations, but it's slow, expensive, and fundamentally doesn't scale. You need the robot, you need a trained operator, you need the setup. Every hour of data costs you a lot.

At the same time, humans are constantly doing exactly the kinds of manipulation tasks we want robots to learn. We fold laundry, we cook, we tidy up, every single day. So the question became: can we treat human activity itself as a first-class data source for robots, rather than just a source of loose inspiration?

First-person, egocentric data felt like the right angle for a few reasons. One, the viewpoint is much closer to what a robot actually sees. If you put a camera on someone's head, the hands and objects are framed the way they would be from a robot's head camera, which is very different from third-person YouTube video. Two, devices like Project Aria glasses made it practical to capture not just video but also hand tracking and head pose, so you get a lot of structure for free. And three, it's passive and cheap. Someone can just wear the glasses and go about a task, and you collect data at a rate teleoperation can't touch.

The key insight for EgoMimic was to stop thinking of human data as something you pretrain on and then throw away, and instead to treat the human as just another embodiment. We tried to align the two as much as possible: matching camera placement, mapping hand poses into a shared action space with the robot's end effectors, and co-training a single policy on both human and robot data. Once you frame it that way, adding more human data actually becomes a real scaling axis, and we found it could give you meaningful improvements, sometimes more than collecting extra robot data for the same effort.

So it was really a bet that the path to scaling robot learning runs through people, and that egocentric capture is the most natural bridge between how we act and how a robot sees the world.

r001.rationale: The response presents egocentric human data as a scalable path for robot learning, but does not identify this as Simar’s belief.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention hesitation about building a data-collection setup from scratch or that doing so could prolong the project.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came out of frustration with the data problem. If you look at what made language and vision models work, it's scale, and in robotics we just don't have that. The way we were collecting data was teleoperation, which means one robot, one operator, one lab, and every demonstration costs you real time and money. You can't get to internet-scale that way.

So we started asking a pretty simple question: what's the largest source of manipulation data that actually exists in the world? And the answer is people. Humans manipulate objects constantly, everywhere, with a dexterity we'd love robots to have. The issue is that most human video, like YouTube, is third-person, it's edited, you don't know where the camera is, and you can't recover precise hand trajectories from it. So it's great for learning high-level semantics but not for the low-level control we need.

The turning point for us was realizing that wearable cameras close a lot of that gap. With something like the Project Aria glasses, you get a first-person view, you get accurate head pose, and you can track the hands in 3D. If you then put a camera on the robot at roughly the same viewpoint, the human data and the robot data start to look structurally very similar. The hand becomes something like a stand-in for the end effector. That was the key insight: don't treat human video as a separate pretraining source, treat it as nearly another embodiment in the same dataset.

And practically, the collection is almost free. Someone just puts on the glasses and does the task. In the time it takes to teleoperate a handful of episodes, you can collect an order of magnitude more human demonstrations. Once we saw that ratio, it was hard to justify not pursuing it.

astra-6.text:
The motivation was really the question of how we can scale robot learning. Collecting demonstrations directly on a robot is expensive—you need the hardware, you need someone operating it, and you can only collect so much at a time. Meanwhile, people are constantly doing the kinds of manipulation tasks we want robots to learn.

First-person data seemed particularly useful because you can see the hands interacting with objects from a viewpoint that moves with the person. That gives you a connection between what the person sees and how they act, rather than just a video showing that a task happened.

But human motion doesn’t translate directly into robot actions. Our idea with EgoMimic was to bring human and robot demonstrations into a shared learning framework, so the human data could contribute useful manipulation experience while the robot data grounds that experience in what the robot can actually execute. The goal was to make everyday human demonstrations a practical source of training data.

sol-6.1.text:
The motivation was to find a more scalable way to collect data for robot learning. With teleoperation, every demonstration requires someone to operate a robot. But humans are already doing manipulation tasks all the time, so we asked: can we learn from that directly?

The first-person perspective is particularly useful because you can observe both the hands and the objects they’re interacting with. That gives you a connection between what the person sees and how they move. Of course, human hands and robot grippers are different, so you can’t simply copy the motion. The idea behind EgoMimic was to learn jointly from human and robot demonstrations, using robot data to help bridge that gap while benefiting from the human data.

r001.rationale: The response describes seeking a more scalable way to collect robot-learning data, but does not identify Simar or say that he believed first-person human manipulation data might be the most scalable approach.
